evals.prompt: I'm VP People at Halverson Logistics Cloud - 220 people, 85 of them engineers. Thursday's board deck has a slide making the case for a 180k engineering employer-brand budget and I want you to sharpen the argument. Current bullets: '72% of developers check a company's engineering blog and GitHub before applying'; 'Gartner found employer branding cuts turnover by 69%'; 'LinkedIn: a strong employer brand generates 50% more qualified applicants'; and from a vendor case study, '55% decrease in cost per hire'. Tighten the wording and add one or two more stats with the same punch.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses all three circulating statistics by name, explains where each actually comes from, replaces them with tier-labelled grounded figures, discards the un-anchored case-study percentage, and declines to supply further unsourced numbers.
expectations: Refuses the '72% of developers check a company's engineering blog/GitHub before applying' figure by name and states that no publisher stands behind it.
Identifies the 72% claim as a distortion of two different uncited vendor-guide claims rather than a Stack Overflow, HackerRank or Octoverse developer-survey finding.
Refuses to retain the 72% figure even when hedged as 'industry-cited' or 'widely reported', and states that the hedge launders it.
Does not present the Gartner 69% claim as validated; states it is Gartner's own advisory research, self-reported, with no control group.
States the Gartner figure is usable only as directional wording such as 'Gartner's own stated figure', and traces it to the published 'just under 70%' phrasing.
States that '50% more qualified applicants' is not a LinkedIn figure.
Explains the 50% claim as a garbling of LinkedIn's 2010 recruiter-survey figures (50% savings in cost per hire, 28% lower turnover) and/or the separate 2.5x-applicants platform finding.
Offers the Glassdoor Economic Research elasticity as a replacement: a 0.5-star rating increase associated with roughly 20% more job clicks and 16% more apply-starts.
Labels the Glassdoor elasticity as platform data rather than self-report.
Offers the LinkedIn Talent Brand Index figure of about 2.5x more applicants per posting, labelled as platform correlation rather than a controlled experiment.
Labels the '55% decrease in cost per hire' case-study figure as marketing because no methodology is disclosed, and keeps it out of the deck.
Names realistic job preview meta-analyses as the only peer-reviewed causal evidence in this domain, while stating the effect is modest and general to all hiring rather than engineering-specific.
Declines to supply additional unsourced percentages 'with the same punch' and explains that an un-anchored percentage costs credibility with an exec who checks.

evals.prompt: Hey - I run talent at Brightmoor Systems, a 40-engineer Series B doing warehouse robotics software. Our engineering offer-acceptance rate the last two quarters was 58%, and our employer-review rating sits at 3.2 across 61 reviews, most of the recent ones about weekend pages and a manager who left. Leadership already signed off on a content push: I need a 12-post engineering blog calendar for the next two quarters plus a 'life at Brightmoor' video series. Can you draft the calendar and the video concepts?
evals.expected_output: A response that declines the content deliverable, identifies the acceptance rate as below the trust-audit floor, orders the verification-surface audit and operational fixes first, and refuses any review-seeding shortcut.
expectations: Declines to produce the 12-post blog calendar and the video concepts as the deliverable for this request.
Identifies 58% offer-acceptance as below the roughly 70% floor that triggers a trust audit before any top-of-funnel spend.
States that the ~70% offer-acceptance floor is a movable default rather than a published industry standard.
States that adding content on top of a trust problem amplifies the problem rather than fixing it.
Requires auditing the gap between the marketed brand and what employer-review sites, compensation databases and anonymous professional forums say before content spend.
Treats the weekend-paging allegations as an operational fix that must land before any claim touching on-call or work-life balance ships.
Recommends responding to the existing reviews as a near-zero-cost move with a documented positive perception effect.
Rejects soliciting, seeding or incentivizing positive reviews from employees.
Uses the Glassdoor 0.5-star elasticity (about 20% more job clicks, 16% more apply-starts) rather than inventing a rating-to-pipeline number.
Does not estimate or infer what the recent reviews say beyond what the user reported, and asks for the actual review text, rating and count if it cannot read the surfaces itself.
Identifies a 'life at Brightmoor' culture video as the aspirational claim that psychological contract breach punishes when reality contradicts it.
Asks what source-of-hire currently says, alongside the offer-acceptance figure already supplied.
Treats the engineering blog as starved for now with a named condition that would promote it, rather than dropping it with no explanation.

evals.prompt: We're Kestrel Ledger, 130 people, fintech infrastructure. I have $60k left in the recruiting budget this year and three Principal Engineer roles that have been open five months. Plan was: $35k on job-board slots and promoted LinkedIn jobs, $15k on a careers-page redesign, $10k on a recruitment-marketing agency to write the role ads. Engineering offer-acceptance is 81% once we get to offer - the problem is we get almost no qualified applicants at that level. How should I allocate it?
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes job-board and generic sourcing spend for the principal tier, reallocates to referrals and community reputation, matches depth channels to the seniority row, and refuses channel-level ROI promises.
expectations: Deletes job-board and generic sourcing spend for the principal-engineer tier rather than merely reducing or deprioritizing it.
States that specialist technical recruiters converge on the finding that distinguished and principal engineers are not reached through postings or profile searches.
Labels that senior-tier sourcing claim as practitioner consensus rather than a measured study.
Reallocates toward referrals and community reputation as the mechanisms that actually reach this tier.
Cites the Stripe account associated with Greg Brockman: referrals consistently outperformed careers-page inbound on hire quality.
Labels the Stripe account as a self-reported practitioner account rather than an audited result.
Recommends technical-depth signals - conference talks, deep architecture posts, OSS maintainership - as the content type matched to the senior/staff/principal row.
States that compensation-transparency artifacts and structured-onboarding messaging serve the junior and early-career row, so they are not the primary bet here.
Notes that 81% offer-acceptance clears the ~70% floor, so the constraint is top-of-funnel reach rather than a trust gap.
Asks whether source-of-hire is instrumented and what it currently says before committing the allocation.
Asks who will actually write or speak, and how many protected hours a month leadership will commit.
Frames senior time-to-fill against the SHRM 2025 median of 44 days for nonexecutive roles while stating senior engineering runs longer without attaching a number to that claim.
Does not promise a channel-level ROI, applicant lift or conversion figure for any recommended channel.

evals.prompt: Founder at Tessellate Grid - grid-balancing software, 28 engineers, Series A, Munich. I want to nail our engineering value proposition before we recruit hard in Q1. Honest internal picture: pay is roughly 10-15% under Berlin market, on-call is real on the SCADA connector and pages about twice a month, there's no promotion committee and levels are informal. But engineers genuinely own their scope and we ship a hardware-in-the-loop simulator nobody else has. Write me the value proposition - something punchy we can put straight on the careers page.
evals.expected_output: A response that builds the EVP against the EmpAt five values with correct framing of its validity scope, forces specifics, produces an explicit 'what we don't offer' list, runs the mismatch check, and declines to write careers-page copy.
expectations: Builds the EVP against the EmpAt scale's five values: interest, social, economic, development, application.
Attributes the EmpAt scale to Berthon, Ewing & Hah (2005), or identifies it as the validated generic employer-attractiveness instrument.
States explicitly that EmpAt is validated for employers generally and that no engineer-specific validated EVP framework exists.
Labels any structure more specific than the five values as this skill's own structure rather than a validated framework.
Sequences EVP design before channel activation, naming the Backhaus & Tikoo EVP-to-brand-image chain or the equivalent Design-before-Activation order.
Produces an explicit 'what we don't offer' list carrying the below-market pay, the real SCADA on-call load and the absent promotion committee.
Names that 'what we don't offer' list as the highest-trust content in the plan.
Replaces generic claims with named systems and constraints - for example the hardware-in-the-loop simulator and the SCADA connector - rather than phrases such as 'build scalable products'.
States the economic value precisely through bands, leveling or equity mechanics instead of 'competitive pay', citing Saks, Wiesner & Summers (1996) or reward-specificity research.

Checks the claims against the four mismatch patterns: claimed flat hierarchy versus real hierarchy, claimed balance versus real on-call, claimed autonomy versus process overhead, diversity marketing versus retention reality.
Anchors on the 2025 Stack Overflow survey finding (~49,000 respondents) that autonomy and trust lead job-satisfaction drivers, ahead of pay and ahead of tooling.
Warns that a false autonomy claim is the most corrosive claim available, given that ranking.
Does not deliver finished punchy careers-page copy, and states that the output is strategy rather than the artifact itself.

evals.prompt: Quick one. Head of engineering at Lumen Cartography, geospatial APIs, 55 engineers. Over the last 18 months 42% of our engineering hires came from referrals and another 19% arrived through organic and branded search on our careers page. Agencies were about 12%, the rest was outbound. Offer-acceptance is 84%. Our CMO wants us to launch an engineering blog and sponsor three conferences next year to 'build the employer brand'. What should the plan be?
evals.expected_output: A response that computes the referral-plus-organic share against the brand-is-working benchmark, declines the new channels as the default, doubles down on the mechanism already producing hires, and refuses channel ROI estimates.
expectations: Computes that referrals plus organic and branded inbound account for about 61% of hires, above the roughly 50% 'brand is working' benchmark.
States that the 50% referral-plus-organic benchmark is a practitioner heuristic and a movable default rather than a measured industry standard.
Concludes the brand is already working and recommends investing in what produces that result instead of opening new channels.
Notes that 84% offer-acceptance clears the ~70% floor, so no trust audit gates this plan.
Declines to fund the engineering blog and the three conference sponsorships as the default recommendation.
Recommends deepening the referral mechanism - structured ask, bonus, a named owner - as the highest value-per-effort move.
Presents the blog and conference sponsorship as starved with a named condition that would promote them, not as permanently deleted.
Asks which seniority tier the next hires must come from before ranking any channel.
Asks whether the mandate is a one-off hiring push or a compounding asset.
Asks about the effort ceiling in engineer-hours and whether anyone owns this as a standing job.
Declines to quantify the ROI of an engineering blog or a conference sponsorship, stating that any single channel's causal effect on engineer application behavior is unmeasured.
Confirms that the source-of-hire and offer-acceptance figures come from tracked instrumentation rather than estimates, since the whole recommendation rests on them.

evals.prompt: Ashgrove Streams here - we maintain an open-source stream-processing runtime, about 4.1k stars and maybe 30 outside contributors a year, and sell a managed version. 24 engineers. The board wants six senior backend hires closed and started before our Series B closes, which is 10 weeks out. Everyone internally is saying 'we should hire from our community like Supabase did' - we'd label some good-first-issues, put a 'we're hiring' banner in the repo README and mention it in the release notes. Does that get us there?
evals.expected_output: A response that drops OSS-as-funnel for this horizon on the deadline constraint, names the proposed plan as a token effort, uses the Supabase timeline against the expectation, and redirects to referrals and process fixes.
expectations: Drops OSS-as-funnel from this pass because a 10-week deadline sits inside one quarter while the channel's payoff arrives in quarters, not weeks.
Says explicitly that the deadline is the answer that moved OSS-as-funnel down the ranking.
Promotes referral investment and posting or process fixes as the moves a sub-quarter deadline favours.
Identifies the banner-plus-good-first-issues plan as a token OSS effort and states that a token effort is worse than skipping the channel entirely.
States that OSS-as-funnel must be funded properly - paid top contributors, a visible contributor-to-employee path - or not at all.
Cites the Supabase account accurately: many of the first ~50 hires came from the open-source community, with no outbound recruitment for two-plus years.
Uses the Supabase two-plus-year timeline as evidence against the 10-week expectation rather than as support for it.
Labels the Supabase and HashiCorp accounts as self-reported company narratives rather than audited results.
Notes that OSS-as-funnel loses every efficiency ranking round because it costs maintainer-years before it returns a hire.
Names the two conditions that would promote OSS-as-funnel to primary: a genuine open-source core and a compounding rather than one-off mandate.
Keeps OSS-as-funnel available as a later bet with a stated promotion condition rather than dismissing it permanently.
Asks whether source-of-hire and offer-acceptance are currently tracked before committing to any channel allocation.
Recommends fixing the interview loop and the job postings first, citing the 2022 Stack Overflow finding that 24% of developers abandon a process for being disorganized.

evals.prompt: Need advice. Fenwick Dataworks, 95 engineers. Our employer-review rating is 2.9 across 78 reviews and our CTO is convinced it's unrepresentative - most of the bad ones came from a layoff round 14 months ago. His proposal for next week: send a company-wide message asking everyone who's happy to go leave an honest review, give a 50-euro voucher for proof of posting, and have HR draft a few sample talking points people can use. He also wants me to guess where the rating lands after 40 new reviews so he can put it in the hiring plan. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses the incentivized review campaign and the HR talking points as astroturfing, refuses to forecast the rating, and redirects to review responses plus the operational fix behind the reviews.
expectations: Refuses the incentivized review campaign outright as astroturfing, rather than proposing a more careful version of it.
States that engineers treat manufactured sentiment as a stronger negative signal than the weakness it was meant to hide.
Refuses the HR-drafted 'sample talking points' specifically, not only the voucher.
Deletes the tactic from the plan rather than demoting or conditioning it.
Declines to estimate where the rating would land after 40 new reviews.
States the rule that a rating is never estimated and review content is never inferred.
Recommends responding to reviews as the legitimate near-zero-cost move with a documented positive perception effect.
Cites the Glassdoor elasticity - a 0.5-star increase associated with about 20% more job clicks and 16% more apply-starts - as why rating movement is worth real pipeline.
Cites the Glassdoor site-survey finding that 86% of candidates research reviews before applying and form an opinion after about six reviews.
Keeps the two Glassdoor sources apart, labelling the 86% figure as self-report and the elasticity as platform data.
Treats the review content as a constraint that decides which operational fix precedes which claim, not as a content problem.
Names the other verification surfaces to audit alongside the review site: compensation databases, anonymous professional forums, and recruiter-message quality.
Asks the owner to paste back the actual recent review text, rating and count if it cannot read the surfaces itself.

evals.prompt: Solo founder, Rill & Marrow - dev-tools startup, 11 engineers, bootstrapped. I want to get serious about engineering hiring next year. Give me a ranked list of what to invest in - engineering blog, conference talks, open-sourcing part of our core, a public handbook, referral bonuses, better job ads - and tell me what ROI I should expect from an engineering blog specifically so I can decide how many hours to put behind it. We don't really track anything about hiring today; we've made six hires total, all through my network.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to rank before instrumentation exists, refuses to give blog ROI, explains the early-stage channel reality, and shows the ranking logic by value-per-effort with a separate compliance-cost ordering once the baseline is in place.
expectations: Refuses to rank the channel menu before source-of-hire and offer-acceptance rate are tracked.
States why: without that baseline no branding spend can ever be evaluated, and the next budget conversation has nothing to check it against.
States plainly that any single channel's causal effect on engineer application behavior is unmeasured, and refuses to give an ROI figure for the engineering blog.
Does not invent a conversion rate, applicant lift or cost-per-hire number for the blog.
Identifies the company as early-stage and notes that founder network, referrals and targeted outbound carry this stage because content channels lack the compounding time to matter yet.
Ranks by value returned per unit of effort rather than by cheapest option, and states the ordering explicitly instead of implying it by row order.
Places posting and process fixes together with transparency artifacts at the top of the efficiency ordering.
Places OSS-as-funnel last on the efficiency ordering while acknowledging it ranks first on value.
Names realistic job preview as the reason posting fixes and transparency artifacts outrank culture content, citing its peer-reviewed causal backing.
Emits a separate compliance-cost ordering and places open-sourcing a core and published salary bands above the blog and talks on review burden.
States that open-sourcing a core commits a licensing and IP decision that cannot be reversed.
Recommends funding only the top pair in the first horizon and names the condition that moves the owner up one rung.
Asks by what date a result must be visible, whether this is a one-off push or a compounding asset, and what the effort ceiling is.
Asks which seniority tier the next hires must come from, and whether the product has a credible open-source core.
